MURDERED BY A NEGRO.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

St. Louis, Mo., Dec. 25.—The little Town of Franklin, a few miles out from here on the Missouri Pacific Road, was the scene of a murder Christmas-Eve, the victim being Henry Speers, one of the road's locomotive engineers. The whole town seems to have celebrated the night in a lively way, and several fights took place before Speers became involved in an altercation with a negro named Andrew Beal. Speers and the negro had several words together, when suddenly the darky was seen to draw a razor out of his bosom and slash Speers with it. The white man cried out for help, and vainly tried to get a revolver out of his pocket. After staggering for a second or two he fell to the ground. The negro, as soon as he had done the cutting, turned and fed out of town into the brush. As the hour was late, and the night very dark, he easily made his escape. Speers was picked up and carried into a grocery store, where his wounds were found to be of a very serious character. His throat was cut, the jugular vein being severed, and there were two or three bad cuts across the windpipe. At first it was thought that there was some hope for him, but he sank rapidly from loss of blood, and a little after 1 o'clock this morning he died. Parties of citizens are today scouring the woods for Beal, who is supposed to be hiding in the vicinity. If he is caught it is probable that no one will ever find out what became of him. The Chief of Police this morning received a telegram from Franklin describing the fugitive murderer as a negro five feet seven inches tall, smooth face, 20 years of age, and the police will be very apt to capture him if he comes to St. Louis.

Three Railway Passengers and a Brakeman Shot. St. Louis, Dec. 25.—A report comes from Neelysville, Butler County, on the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern Railway, that while a passenger train was there yesterday a man from St. Louis, whose name is not given, shot R. P. Jones and wife of Smith's Ferry, Beaver County, Pa., and Dr. J. H. Rogers of Orell, Texas, and then escaped to the woods. All were passengers on the train. Mrs. Jones is dangerously wounded in the head. Her husband was shot in the hand, and Dr. Rogers received a severe flesh wound in the shoulder. Mr. Jones and his wife were left in Corning in care of the railroad agent, and Dr. Rogers continued his journey to Texas. The affair seems to be involved in great mystery. A despatch from Pacific, Mo., says Andrew Beal, a negro, shot and killed Pat Crow, a switch brakeman at that place, last night. BANKING AND FINANCIAL.

A disorderly character at Ausonia, Conn., inflicted fatal wounds upon Chief of Police Hayes, who sought to arrest him.

One hundred citizens of Munfordville, Ky., have strung to a tree two negroes accused of robbing and nearly murdering J. A. Gardner. One of the lynched men confessed the crime.

At Avon, Ind., on Christmas eve, Rodolphus Caywood shot Edmund Faxett for the seduction of his sister, who is about to become a mother.

AFTER a Christmas eve night at the railroad town at Franklin, Mo., Andrew Beal, a young negro, killed Henry Speers, an engineer, with a razor. The murderer fled in the direction of St. Louis, followed by a competent lynching party.

An unknown fiend fired shots into a smoking-car on the Iron Mountain railway, at Neeleyville, Mo., on Friday night, and escaped into the forest. Dr. J. H. Paine, of Carroll, Tex., was killed, and P. P. Jones and wife, from Pennsylvania, mortally wounded.

A dispute arose on the 24th at a supper table at a boarding house in New Alexandria, Ohio, near Steubenville, and Dr. Henry, a dentist, attacked Dr. Schooley, a prominent young physician of Mount Pleasant. A wealthy farmer named Buckingham took Henry's part, when Schooley drew a revolver and put a ball through Buckingham's head, inflicting a probably fatal wound. Henry seized a shovel and beat Schooley about the head, wounding him so that he cannot recover. They are all of the best citizens of Jefferson county.

The railroad to the city of Mexico begins to look like a sure thing. A banking house in New York has advertised that it will receive bids for seven and a half millions in bonds and seven and a half in shares for the proposed construction of a railroad from the city of Mexico to Laredo, on the Rio Grande, where it will meet the American system. The distance is 750 miles. The route is generally favorable, and it could be constructed for that sum if there is no stealing on the part of the officers and the contractors.

A LEADING Boston dry-goods house will doubtless be made to suffer for the blunder of its private detective. A day or two ago a wealthy lady, wife of an iron manufacturer of the city, was in the store making purchases when she was suddenly accosted by the private detective who asked for the things she had stolen. Notwithstanding her protestations of innocence and her offer to prove her respectability, she was arrested and searched, and handed over to the police. It seems that a cheap collar, worth 30 cents, had become attached to the fringe on her cloak sleeve and on this the arrest was based. It is understood that the husband has instructed a lawyer to proceed with a suit against the house. All names are withheld at present.

ELECTRIC BRIEFS.
WILLIAMSBURGH, O., December 15. —The chair factory of S. D. Mount, just completed at a cost of $8000, was completely destroyed by fire today.

GREENSBURGH, Ind., December 15. —Mrs Sarah Vassar was accidentally shot last night by a boarder, Miss Athey. Her wound is not fatal.

CHAMPAIGN, Ill., December 15. —Henry Spears and Wm. Gray were suffocated while digging a well near this place yesterday.

WASHINGTON, December 15. —A dispatch from Fort Buford to the war department says that Sitting Bull will undoubtedly surrender with his whole command before ten days. He has expressed his determination to do so.

NEW YORK, December 15. —Two bad cases of small-pox have been discovered among Italian immigrants, who arrived in the steamer Italia, and everybody on board was quarantined in consequence.

LYNCHBURG, Va., December 15. —Three male negroes were sold for $4 at public auction at Liberty, Bedford county, Monday, by order of a magistrate under an old vagrant law. Absolute ownership was given, closing at the expiration of three months.

NEW YORK, December 15. —Martha Terhune, a spinster of New Jersey, has just died after fasting eleven weeks on scarcely anything and fifty-nine days on absolutely nothing.

NEW YORK, December 15. —The Erie and New York Central roads have reduced their Castle Garden immigrant fares to the west twenty per cent, to meet the Pennsylvania cut in races.

FRANKLIN, Tenn., December 15. Charles Reese cut John Harper's throat at a ball, near this place, last night, killing him instantly, and Henry Murray cut Bill Winstead through the right leg, Saturday night. All of the above are colored.

SANTA FE, N. M., December 15 — Monday night a double murder occurred here. Charles Bonsail, a young American, shot and killed two Mexicans and wounded two others, one fatally. He then made his escape.

Mrs. O. J. Turk, a school teacher at Wayne, Mich., was run over and killed by the lightning express train on the Michigan Central, yesterday evening.

Mrs. Bergman, the young wife who left her home in Philadelphia some time since, in a creaky fit of infatuation for a young Spaniard, is still detained in New York, and refuses to return home with her relatives.

The Irish colony at Connemara,

Minn., are undergoing fearful sufferings from cold and hunger. They have neither wood or coal, and have been compelled to resort to hay for fuel. Many of the colonists are badly frozen, and their destitution has brought on much sickness. Several families have been sleeping on hay couches all winter. Unless speedy aid is sent them many must perish. Some of the peasants say they were better off in Ireland, where they at least had plenty of potatoes.

Yesterday was the second day of the sale of Chicago's new city bonds, and over $270 000 worth were taken. This is about half of the entire amount issued.

El. Long, colored, will be hanged in Jackson, Tenn., next Friday, for the murder of Rogers last June. Long loved Rogers' wife, and in order to possess her killed him.

Zeidenberg & Co., the largest manufacturers and importers of cigars and tobacco in New York, announced on yesterday that they would be compelled to suspend business. The announcement caused much excitement among the trade. The failure is attributed to the shrinkage in the value of tobacco.

Mile. Jeanne Bernhardt, sister of Sarah, arrived in New York yesterday in a French steamer from Havre. She left immediately for Boston, where her sister is playing. In appearance Jeanne resembles her sister in a striking degree.

Henry Williams, a machinist on the Southern railroad, and well connected, was found with his skull crushed and his pockets turned inside out, in Cincinnati yesterday evening.

Aaron Morris and Bertha Gardner, of Selma, Clark county, O., both about eighteen years old, were arrested yesterday on suspicion of elope ment in Cincinnati, and returned home last night. The girl says that the whole cause of the trouble is that an uncle of hers wants to marry her, and caused their arrest to thwart Morris' plan. The Alliance, the organ of Prof Swing and his Central church, of Chicago, is reported to be in financial straits. Henry L Shepherd has re signed the management, and Prof Swing is soon to sever his connection

A CORRESPONDENT visiting the Connemara colony in the Northwest, confirms former reports of the great suffering of those people. There is suffering from food, sickness, lack of medicine, fuel, bedding, etc., throughout the entire colony. Frozen potatoes and corn meal is all they have to eat, upon which they could manage to get along, the correspondent says, had they sufficient fuel and clothing. The winter is very severe, and their suffering must consequently be very great.

One of the coolest and most deliberate suicides on record is reported from Shelbina, Mo. An old negro named Cy. Arne, going to a woods, cut a wits of bittersweet, and attempted to hang himself with that but it broke. Then he made another of hickory and twisted it to form a loop, which he slipped over his head. When found he was standing on his feet, his body bent forward, the weight coming on the loop. He could have relieved himself at any time by reaching up to the projecting limb just above his head. He bent twigs back to keep them out of the way.

HENRY WILLIAMS, of Ludlow, Ky., a railroad man, started to cross the river to Cincinnati to buy some Christmas presents. A half hour after he left his home, (at 5:30 p. m.) he was found lying in an insensible condition at an alley entrance, his skull cracked and pockets turned inside out. At his feet was lying an iron pin two feet long. The murder was traced to a negro living just back of Ludlow, and a vigilance committee attempted to take the fellow out and hang him, but failed in the attempt.

A DOUBLE murder has just occurred at Lajoya, N. M. Charles Bonsail, a young American from Albuquerque, had opened a store at the place about two days before. That night he was at the house of a Mexican, and speaking to a girl in the house, was told by her brother to let her alone and not speak to her. This led to a quarrel, in which Bonsail shot and killed two Mexicans, named Jesus Maria Bariela and Jose Ignacio Bariela, and wounding also two other Mexicans, one of them, Sylvester Esquibel, fatally. He then made his escape. A posse of thirty men are looking for him, and when captured his chances for immediate lynching are more than good.

A WOMAN who had been in the service of the family of Dr. C. C. Graham, of Louisville, as a servant for a long term of years, died of old age last week, and was buried in Cave Hill Cemetery. Two medical students went to raise her for the dissecting table, and by mistake got into the wrong cemetery. Selecting what they took to be the grave of the old lady, they bagan digging. After digging to the depth of about two feet one of them received a shot in the leg, and hallowing "ouch," tumbled into the grave, while his pal made good his escape by rapid strides. The wounded ghoul remained in the grave until helped out by the Sexton, who, in the kindness of his heart, sent him on his way rejoicing. Who the young men were could not be ascertained, the Cemetery authorities trying to hush the matter up.

Everything worked like greased machinery until the arrival of some visitors from Scranton by the 11 o'clock freight train, which created a ripple of excitement that soon subsided.
